Question: Do Americans think European football is stupid the same way Europeans think American football is stupid?
Answer: I fucking hate soccer, AKA “European football”. It's kind of like hockey… if you removed everything exciting about hockey and made it excruciatingly dull to watch. On top of that, soccer players in general are so soft they make even baseball players look tough. Seriously, these guys stub a toe and they're rolling around on the ground like they got shot. (Then you have hockey players, especially the Canadians — Dan Girardi once played three rounds of the playoffs on a broken foot, and Glenn Healy took a slapshot to the throat in goal, sat on the bench for five minutes to catch his breath, then played the rest of the game — and won.) I have no idea why it's so popular. It's an insanely boring sport. Fun to play, but painful to watch. Having said that, I also hate American football, and it's a punishment to me to have to watch it every Thanksgiving. The only sport I really like is ice hockey, although basketball at least is exciting and fast-paced, and baseball at the pro level has a sort of Zen element to it that can be intriguing. Watching a pitcher on the mound can be fascinating. Both American and European football, however, suck.

Question: Why do people keep naming their children the same old common names like John, Michael, Anthony, Alex, Sophia, Anne, Sarah and Mary and what kind of name would you choose if you had a kid?
Answer: Some names are timeless and will never go out of style. A name like Michael is classic; you can find Michaels of any age. You can go by Michael, or Mike, Mikey, Mick, or, as my 20-something cousin does, Mickey. Generally speaking, nobody has to ask how to spell or pronounce it. It's a sturdy, dependable name. So are William, Anne, and Sarah. You have to remember that your kid doesn't just have to live with their name as a kid, they're going to be stuck with it all their lives (unless they decide to go to the hassle of legally changing it), so why saddle them with something trendy or, worse, super unusual? Studies have shown that people with unusual names have a harder time finding employment, and even are more likely to be incarcerated. I'm not saying it's fair to allow a name to influence your decision to hire or not hire someone, but it happens nonetheless. Names also go in and out of style like other fashion trends. 30 years ago, nobody outside of Ireland or maybe the UK named their sons Aidan — the only Aidan I'd ever heard of growing up was the actor Aidan Quinn (who is American, but whose parents were from Ireland). In 1990, it wasn't even in the top 1,000 baby names in the U.S. Ten years later, it was in the top ten, while today, it's still top 25, and it's no longer an unusual name at all. Aidan is a more common name for American baby boys today than John, Anthony, or Alex. It's also funny that, at least in the U.S., the only one of the names you listed that's in the top ten most popular for either boys or girls is Sophia. Mary is actually a very uncommon name for American babies these days, not even top 100. Naming your kid Mary is more against the grain than naming her Harper or Amelia — both of which are top ten names in the United States. If I had a kid — I do not and never will — for a boy I've always liked Alexander, James, and Thomas. I'd also have considered Edward, after my dad and brother, although Eddie is my pet rabbit's name. For a girl, perhaps the name I was almost given, Alexandra (assuming I didn't already have a son named Alex), or possibly Kathleen after my mother, although an Irish name like Kathleen doesn't go very well with my Italian surname, and my mom went by Kay, which is another name I like. But you'd never catch me naming my kid Harper or Ava, or that current plague of a name for boys, Liam. I'd sooner go with Mary or John.

Question: What is a rabbit proof heating mat? I want 2 rabbits and I would keep them in an insulated shed outside. It gets quite cold where I live so they would need it to be heated.
Answer: Please don't get rabbits if you're planning on keeping them outside. They will not be happy living outdoors in a cold climate, and subject not only to extreme cold and heat, but to predators, parasites, toxins, insects (especially fly strike) and diseases like tularemia, myxomatosis, and RHD. Even a predator that can't actually get into a rabbit's hutch or enclosure can still frighten it enough to kill it via a heart attack. Studies have shown that outdoor rabbits have an average lifespan of about 3–4 years, whereas indoor rabbits average 8–12. I will never understand keeping pet rabbits outdoors. What's the point of even having them? You're not going to have the kind of bond with them that you would if they lived indoors, because you'll be living in separate spaces. I mean, why do you want rabbits? So you can stick them in a shed in your backyard and just leave them there? Maybe visit them once or twice a day? I just don't see the fulfillment in that setup. Pet rabbits are not livestock, they don't take up that much space, and they're no less hygienic or more destructive than the average dog or cat. (In fact, they're significantly cleaner than the average dog.) Housing rabbits outdoors is a holdover from their days as livestock; it's outdated and unnecessary. In the 21st century, pretty much every animal welfare organization, especially in the U.S., advises keeping pet rabbits indoors. Otherwise they're not really pets. They're just animals that live in your yard. Keep them indoors and you don't need to worry about keeping them warm in cold weather. If you can't keep them indoors, don't get rabbits, especially if you live in a cold climate. (EDIT: I just want to add that I know there are cultural differences in different countries, but the general attitude has absolutely been changing. In recent years I have seen terrific indoor rabbit setups in many countries where it's usually more common to house rabbits outdoors, including the UK, Australia, India, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, U.A.E., and Sudan.)

Question: What are some peculiar requests that actors or actresses make?
Answer: Back in the 1960s and 70s, when he was perhaps the biggest movie star in the world, Steve McQueen had a habit of demanding free items in bulk from studios as a condition of appearing in their films, usually regular, day-to-day items like blue jeans, electric razors, and other common hygiene products. McQueen would then donate the items to the California Junior Boys' Republic (today just called Boys' Republic), a reform school in Chino Hills, California. As a troubled youth who had endured a tumultuous, abusive childhood, and had numerous brushes with the law beginning as early as age 9, McQueen had been remanded to the school by his mother and stepfather as a teen, and credited it with helping him turn his life around. He was also known to visit the school periodically to spend time talking to the boys and playing pool with them, even after becoming an A-list star. McQueen was not a saint — he absolutely had his vices and his unlovely character traits — but he wasn't all bad. EDIT: To the people asking why he didn't use “his own money” for charity, um, he did. The items were part of his negotiated salary, and none of the studios had to provide them if they didn't really want to. More importantly, you negative Nancies don't seem to grasp that McQueen also donated his time to the boys at the school, which to me is more valuable than money. Any rich asshole can throw money at a cause, they do it every day. They don't all actually hang out with troubled kids and try to make a personal, positive impact on them.
